the formal opening of the Convention. President Stanley King

1. Resolved: That the Recorder be directed to write an ex
pression of gratitude to President King of Amherst College for his
welcome to the Convention on behalf of the College.
2. Resolved: That this Convention hereby express to Amherst
College its appreciation for its cordial hospitality and generous ex
tension of campus facilities to the delegates and alumni.

3. Resolved: That the delegates and members, assembled in
Convention in the 108th year of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity, extend
their gratitude to the Gamma Chapter, its undergraduates and
alumni, for the cordial reception extended to those attending the
Convention.
4. Resolved: That the Convention is grateful to the members
of the Executive Council, and the officers of the Council, for their
untiring efforts on behalf of the Chapters and the Fraternity as a
whole.
5. Resolved: That the Convention hereby records its appre
ciation of the unselfish and effective efforts of the Board of Gover
nors of the Alumni Association, and its officers.
6. Resolved: That the delegates to this Convention convey to
the Council's Advisory Committee on the Diamond, and to the
members of the Editorial Staff, their thanks and appreciation for
the excellent work done during the year.
7. Resolved: That this Convention hereby expresses to the
Council's Advisory Committee on the Annals, and to the Secretary
and Archivist, its gratitude for the untiring and unselfish services
rendered in the compilation of this volume.
8. Resolved: That the Recorder be directed to send telegrams
of greeting from the Convention to each of the past Presidents of
the Executive Council : Earl D. Babst, Iota 1893 ; Edward L.
Stevens, Chi 1899; Archibald Douglas, Lambda 1894.
9. Resolved: That the delegates to this Convention express to
Brother Scott Turner, Phi '02, President of the Executive Council
of the Psi Ppsilon Fraternity, and President of this Convention,
their appreciation for his work in presiding over all the sessions of
this Convention, and for the able manner in which he has conducted
the meetings.
10. Resolved: That the delegates to this Convention express
their gratitude to all the Officers of this Convention and to the
Committees reporting to the Convention, for the efficient manner in
which they have handled the work allotted to them.
11. Resolved: That the delegates to this Convention extend
their gratitude to Judge Hammond for his cordial hospitality and
generous extension of his grounds for the Convention picnic.
Upon motion duly made, seconded and passed, the report of the Com

THE ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
OF THE
EXECUTIVE COUNCIL
TO THE
1941 CONVENTION OF PSI UPSILON
HELD UNDER THE AUSPICES OF THE
EXECUTIVE COUNCIL AND THE GAMMA CHAPTER
Amherst. Massachusetts
September 4. 5 and 6, 1941
The Executive Council cordially welcomes the delegates of our twentyseven Chapters to this Convention held in the one hundred and eighth
year of our Fraternity.
We are also celebrating the one hundredth anniversary of the Gamma
Chapter, our host at this Convention. We and all other members .of Psi
Upsilon congratulate the Gamma upon passing this milestone in its career.
We rejoice in its long record of solid achievement. We are proud of its
many distinguished alumni, and of its present strength and splendid esprit
de corps.
We voice our sincere thanks to the undergraduates, alumni, and Con
vention Committees of the Gamma, for the thoughtful and generous ar
rangements made to promote the success of this Convention and to entertain
all who attend it.
We likewise wish to express our gratitude to Amherst College, its
President, Dr. Stanley King, and its Board of Trustees for hospitably
making available to our delegates the buildings and facilities of the College.
Chapter Visits :
Since our last Convention the following eight official visits have been
made by members of the Executive Council :
Theta Herbert J. Flagg
Delta Francis N. Bangs
Gamma Harold L. Berry
Upsilon Francis N. Bangs
Pi Frederick S. Fales
Beta Beta Edward T. Richards
Epsilon Phi Roswell G. Ham
Nu Henry N. Woolman
Page Fifteen

PSI UPSILON FRATERNITY
In addition, under appointment of the Executive Council pursuant to
General Resolution No. 3 of the Convention of 1939, Brother Frederick
C. Broadfoot. Nu '06, made an official visit to the Theta Theta.
Informal visits were also made to several other chapters.
The Condition of the Fraternity :
As yet Psi Upsilon has not received the full impact of the crisis
through which the world is passing.
Even in Canada, for two years a belligerent in the war, severe inroads
have not been made upon our undergraduate membership. Although some
of our Canadian undergraduates have joined the armed forces, in general,
student enlistment is not thus far being encouraged by the authorities.
On the other hand, some types of courses are being shortened, and, to
expedite graduation, curtailment of vacations has been proposed. Also,
many of the younger alumni of our Canadian chapters have for some time
been in aviation, military, or naval service. To them our hearts go out.
We know they will bravely meet every ordeal that may confront them.
We hope that each one of them shall come through to the end safely.
For all fraternity chapters, the years immediately ahead may prove
crucial. Psi Upsilon enters upon them concious of its strength. But for
no chapter should there be overconfidence. Drastic social and financial
adjustments threaten. The average undergraduate is likely to have far
less to spend after caring for his bare necessities. When considering
joining a fraternity, he may well hold back and be critical of values to be
received. At the same time, taxes and costs of commodities�
such as coal
and food�
may increase. Furthermore, under the Selective Service Act
of the United States, many upper classman may be forced to leave college
for military service, thus depriving our chapters of their natural leaders
and adding to their financial problems.
To meet possible additional costs, it obviously will be necessary either
to increase revenues through added membership, to raise dues of present
members, or to curtail overhead. Maintenance of membership by Psi
Upsilon must not be permitted to become difficult because of financial
factors. Therefore, it would seem best for each chapter to make prompt
efforts to reduce running overhead.
One of our younger chapters�the Delta Delta�under the guidance
of a particularly active group of alumni officers, has this year endeavored
to anticipate these financial problems. It has already succeeded in de
creasing its fixed' annual charges by over $800. This was accomplished
through procuring a reduction on its real-estate assessment, and reductions
of interest-rates on mortgage indebtedness. In addition, the Delta Delta
has made further substantial savings in operating overhead�particularly
in connection with the board department�through the installation of a
cost-analysis and budget-control system which, under close alumni surveil
lance and with the guidance of an unusually enterprising undergraduate
Page Sixteen

RECORDS OF THE C ONVENTION
treasurer, produced most satisfactory results. An operating deficit of a
prior year was thus transformed into a substantial surplus. The same
chapter is now endeavoring to raise a reserve fund of several thousand
dollars as insurance against contingencies during any war emergency.
The business administration and financial setup of each of our other
chapters might well be studied to the end that the cost of membership in
Psi Upsilon may be kept as low at each college as the particular situation
may permit.
In the last several months, our Lambda Chapter has reached a most
important decision. For many years it occupied the same chapter house
which was its home during the last college year. The financial problem
of doing so, in an institution in which fraternity membership must be
drawn largely from day-students, has recently become increasingly difficult.
The burden of high wages and unusually heavy municipal taxes was aug
mented by repeated demands from city authorities for substantial altera
tions to comply with group-housing laws. Alumni had a number of times
contributed to overcome emergencies. It was believed, however, that the
financial uncertainties were handicapping the chapter in rushing campaigns,
and that no solution could be satisfactory or permanent which did not
reduce chapter overhead to a point where it could be easily met out of
readily-obtainable chapter income. Taking these factors into consideration,
the Lambda reached the important decision of surrendering its chapter
house and of procuring specially-equipped quarters in one of the univer
sity's dormitories. This new arrangement, it is believed, will permit the
Lambda to offer to its members the advantages which go with fraternity
membership at a greatly reduced cost, and at the same time will substan
tially broaden the field of its choice of new members. We commend the
Lambda's trustees upon their courage and their realism, and wish the
chapter every success as it carries on under the new conditions.
Adjusting chapter finances to changing conditions is only a part of the
problem. Adding new members under the situation which may confront
us may more easily be accomplished if we also concentrate on the task
of making membership in Psi Upsilon thoroughly worthwhile, and of
seeing to it that each chapter is a constructive force in developing and
bringing out in each member his best traits and abilities. Only by so doing
may Psi Upsilon be a real factor in the educational efforts of the colleges
and universities at which it is represented. The National Interfraternity
Conference has stated its conclusions, in which we heartily agree, as
follows :
"Isn't this then the National Defense Program of the Fraternities?
To do our full share toward helping our undergraduate members to
qualify for the enormous responsibilities which await the college men
of today; to merge selfish ambitions, prestige, and all the superficialities
of fraternity life in solicitude for the national need; to remember that
America cannot avoid playing a big part in world affairs during the

than ever before for larger responsibilities; and to be determined that

National Interfraternity Conference:
Pursuant to the authority granted at the 1940 Convention Psi Upsilon
became a member of the National Interfraternity Conference. Our
President, Scott Turner, has participated actively in the work of the
Conference, serving on its Executive Committee and on its Committee on
Policy.
The contacts with leaders of other fraternities have proven quite
helpful, and much valuable information has been derived regarding local
problems at particular universities, as well as regarding various problems
affecting fraternities in general.
The Constitution :
No chapter having made objection following notification of the amend

Convention, such amendment is now in full force and effect.

purpose.
The Diamond:
This year has again seen the publication of a successful and outstand
ing fraternity magazine. Much praise is due to Brother John A. Cooper.

balance of the publication year.
Scholarship :
Scholarship continues to be one of Psi Upsilon's chief problems. Dur
ing the last year, chapter after chapter has been ranked in the lower half
of the scholastic list of fraternities on its campus. Every effort should be
made in each chapter to see that the scholastic efforts of members are
conscientious and well directed.

The Alumni Association of Psi Upsilon:
During the past year the Alumni Association has performed outstand
ing work.
In November, the Association did all of the work in connection with
the allotment of seats to members of Psi Upsilon at the National Inter
fraternity Conference Dinner held in New York on November 29, 1940.
The Association also arranged for the holding of a Psi Upsilon banquet
in New York City on April 18. 1941. at which 166 brothers gathered for
a most enjoyable evening of Psi Upsilon fellowship.
The most outstanding task, however, was in connection with the Annals
of Psi Upsilon. The Association shouldered the financial and clerical
burden of circularizing the general membership of the fraternity for sub
scriptions and undertook other tasks in connection with the subscriptionlist. It also prepared and edited the list of living members contained in
the volume. In this connection, the address-lists of the approximately
fourteen thousand living members of Psi Upsilon have been brought into
better condition than ever before. They are arranged alphabetically, by
classes, and geographically, and the great majority of addresses are up-todate and correct.

Report of the Treasurer
1941
There is presented herewith a comparative statement of the net worth
of the various funds of the Fraternity held by the Executive Council as
of April 30, 1940 and 1941. A list of investments held in the General
Fund, the Bridgman Fund and the Diamond Life Subscription Fund,
showing the cost and market value, is also presented.
The cash position of the Fraternity continues favorable. The situation
with respect to acounts receivable, however, is the worst that it has been
in years, as three chapters�namely the Zeta, the Lambda, and the Zeta
Zeta�
have not paid their undergraduate dues and Diamond life subscrip
tions for the past college year. The situation with respect to our invest
ments remains bad. We have an unrealized loss on our securities, based
on April 30th market values, of almost $12,000. If our investments were
carried in the statement at market value instead of at cost, the aggregate
net worth of the funds of the Fraternity would work out as $30,633.51.
Included among our liabilities is a reserve of $5,550 for Diamond Life
Subscriptions. This reserve has been accumulated in 1940 and 1941. The
accumulation of this reserve is an improvement over the preceding practice
when no reserves were set up, and Diamond Life Subscription moneys
were spent for the current running expenses of the Diamond. The cur
rent Diamond Fund showed a loss of $2,880.96 in 1941, which was covered
by transfers of $2,300 from the Bridgman Fund and $600 from the General
Fund.
The Income and expense accounts of tbe various funds are selfexplanatory. The General Fund had a surplus of $667.87 after an appro
priation of $498.85 to write down the carrying value of Directories pub
lished in 1931. It is to be hoped that the carrying value of these Direc
tories can be entirely amortized over the next few years. As mentioned
above. $600 of this surplus in the General Fund was' transferred to meet
a part of the deficit for printing the Diamond.
The Secretary and Treasurer of the Fraternity are Trustees of a fund
known as the Willard Fiske Fund, the assets on which are not shown in
the attached statement. This fund was started by a gift of $50 made in
1881 by Willard Fiske, who stipulated that the money should be kept
intact until the fund reaches $1,000, when the income thereon becomes
available for the general purposes of the Fraternity. The fund now
amounts to $662.91, which is deposited in two savings bank accounts.
